title: Extension manifests carry `tainted` and `secret` qualifiers; an extension can only tighten
scope:
how `rule:security/tainted-qualifier`'s and
`rule:security/secret-qualifier`'s compile-time qualifiers behave at a Tier 1
extension call site, and what the `nvs.manifest`/WIT world must be able to express. Not in scope: the
rest of the WIT world's shape, which M8 authors.

summary.headline: An extension can declare its inputs and outputs more restricted, never safer
summary.body:
Untrusted input keeps its marking through every extension call without the extension declaring
anything: a result computed from a tainted argument is tainted. A manifest may declare only two
departures, and both tighten: a parameter can refuse tainted values, and a return can be
declared always tainted. No manifest can declare that an extension cleans a value; only a `Core`
function whose contract names one specific destination may do that. Secrets do not cross an
extension boundary at all. A hostile manifest can make an extension harder to call but never
opens a hole.
